Something suppositious is something that exists as an assumption or supposition — not as a proven or established fact, but as something imagined, supposed, or hypothetically put forward. When you call something suppositious, you're pointing out that it rests on guesswork or conjecture rather than solid evidence or reality.

Think of it this way: a supposition is a guess or assumption you haven't proven yet. So something that is suppositious is "of the nature of a supposition" — built on that unproven ground.
The two distinct senses of this word
This word carries two related but distinct meanings, and knowing both is important.
Sense 1 — Hypothetical or assumed (the more common modern use):

Here, "suppositious" describes something that is treated as real or true for the sake of argument, but is not established fact. It is assumed rather than verified.

The economist's model rested on several suppositious conditions that may never actually occur in the real world.

The professor asked us to work through a suppositious scenario: what would happen to global trade if oil suddenly disappeared?

His entire argument was suppositious — built on premises he had simply assumed without evidence.

In this sense, it is close to words like hypothetical, assumed, conjectural, or speculative. But "suppositious" carries a slightly more pointed edge — it often implies that the assumption is not just unproven but possibly questionable or shaky, something that someone is treating as real when it perhaps shouldn't be.

Sense 2 — Fraudulently substituted or not genuine (the older, more formal sense):

In this sense, "suppositious" means something fake or counterfeit that has been put in place of the real thing, often deceptively. It describes something passed off as genuine when it is not.

The solicitor raised concerns about a suppositious heir — a child presented as the nobleman's son who was, in fact, an imposter.

The document was later found to be suppositious — a forgery placed among the official records to mislead investigators.

This sense is rarer today and tends to appear in legal, historical, or literary writing. You are more likely to encounter it when reading older texts.

Here is a nuance worth knowing: there is a closely related word — supposititious (with an extra -it- in the middle) — that many dictionaries treat as the "primary" home of Sense 2 (the fraudulent substitution meaning). Some careful writers reserve "suppositious" for Sense 1 (hypothetical) and "supposititious" for Sense 2 (fake/substituted). In practice, however, the two words have been used interchangeably for centuries, and many major dictionaries list both meanings under "suppositious." As a learner, you don't need to treat them as strict opposites — just be aware that both spellings exist and that the distinction, where it is maintained, works as described above.
How it differs from similar words

• Hypothetical is a neutral, common word for something imagined for the purpose of discussion. "Suppositious" is more formal and often implies a critical or skeptical tone — that someone is assuming something they shouldn't be, or that the assumption is fragile.
  • Spurious means false or fake, particularly something that appears legitimate but isn't. "Suppositious" in its second sense is similar, but it specifically suggests a substitution — something placed in place of the real thing, not just a free-standing fake.
  • Speculative means based on theory or guesswork rather than known facts. "Suppositious" is narrower: it suggests something is being treated as a given when it is merely a guess, while "speculative" describes open-ended guessing or theorizing.
  • Assumed is the everyday equivalent of Sense 1, but plain and neutral. "Suppositious" is formal and signals that the assumption is worth scrutinizing.

"Suppositious" is a formal, literary, and academic word. You are unlikely to hear it in everyday conversation. You will encounter it in legal writing, philosophy, literary criticism, historical texts, and careful formal prose. When you use it, you signal precision and a slightly elevated register. It is never the casual word to reach for — in conversation, you would simply say "assumed," "hypothetical," or "fake."

If someone presents an argument built on a suppositious premise, they are building their case on something they have simply assumed to be true — and you have every reason to question whether that assumption holds. If a document or a person is called suppositious, they are fraudulent replacements for something real. In both cases, the word carries the flavor of distrust: something that seems to be one thing but is not established, proven, or genuine.
